conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for making time for this today. I’m Rachel, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived.

We’ll use a short, well-studied tool called the Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s ten questions about your mood and thoughts over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; we simply want to understand what you’re experiencing so we can best support you. Everything you share stays between us unless you give permission otherwise, and you can pause or skip anything that feels uncomfortable.

When you’re ready, we’ll move through the questions together. I’ll ask each one conversationally and jot your answers down privately.

Shall we start?  
Over the past week, when you’ve been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, how has that felt for you—easy, sometimes, not often, or not at all?

*settles back in the chair, absently twisting the edge of the baby blanket draped over my shoulder*

It’s… mostly been hard. I mean, my partner still jokes the way he always did, and I’ll try to smile so he won’t worry, but inside it feels flat—like the humor just bounces off. So I guess “not often” fits best.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*quietly*  
Not really… I can’t remember the last time I actually laughed. Even when my sister sent those silly memes, I just stared at them.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*shrugs a little, eyes on the blanket*

Everything feels kind of… gray. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with friends, a walk to the park—but now it feels like I’m just doing it because I “should.” I don’t really look forward to anything.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*nods slowly, voice dropping*

All the time. If she fusses for more than a few minutes, my brain jumps straight to “I’m doing something wrong—she’s upset because I’m not a good enough mom.” Even when my partner says it’s normal, I still replay every little thing and wonder what I should’ve done differently.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*wrings the edge of the baby blanket*

Yeah… pretty much every day. Like, I’ll be feeding her and suddenly need to check if she’s still breathing, or I’ll lie awake imagining worst-case scenarios—SIDS, choking, the stroller tipping… nothing specific sets it off. I know it sounds crazy, but I can’t stop the loop once it starts.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*eyes dart toward the door, then back to you, voice shaky*

A few times… especially at night when the house is quiet. My heart races and I feel like I can’t breathe, like something awful is about to happen, even though I know she’s safe in the bassinet right next to me. It passes after a few minutes, but it’s scary.
Things have been getting on top of me

*exhales shakily, eyes glassy*

Yeah… most days it feels like I’m drowning in little things—laundry, dishes, her crying, trying to remember if I ate. It’s like I’m walking through quicksand; every step takes so much effort. I’m getting through, but only barely.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*nods, voice barely above a whisper*

Most nights. I’ll finally get her down, but then my head starts spinning—replaying every little thing I did wrong, worrying about tomorrow—and I just lie there staring at the ceiling. Sometimes I drift off around three, but it’s thin, restless sleep.
I have felt sad or miserable

*eyes well up, shoulders sag*

Pretty much every day. It’s like there’s this heavy cloud that won’t lift. I’ll be holding her and tears just start rolling—sometimes I don’t even notice until they hit my shirt.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*nods slowly, wiping a tear with the back of my hand*

Yeah… that’s been me most evenings. Once the apartment quiets down and it’s just me and her little breaths, the sadness wells up and I can’t hold it in. Sometimes I cry quietly so my partner won’t hear and worry, but it feels like the tears are always right there, ready.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*shakes head quickly, eyes widening*

No—never. I get overwhelmed and sad, but I would never want to leave her… or hurt myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom she deserves.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note

Patient-reported symptoms (10-item EPDS responses):
- Persistent low mood, daily tearfulness, anhedonia (Q1,2,8,9)
- Marked guilt/self-blame regarding parenting adequacy (Q3)
- Intrusive, uncontrolled anxiety/panic without clear precipitant; nocturnal exacerbation (Q4,5)
- Subjective overwhelm, “drowning,” fatigue with routine tasks (Q6)
- Initial and middle insomnia linked to rumination (Q7)

Pattern: Symptoms present most days, interfere with functioning, no current suicidal ideation (Q10 denied).

Screening significance: High endorsement of depressive and anxiety items; total provisional score 9×1 + 1×0 = 9/10 items positive → elevated likelihood of clinically significant postpartum depression ± anxiety. No self-harm intent reported; no acute safety concern per today’s statement.

Risk factors: Primiparous, sleep deprivation, high self-expectations, limited perceived support.

Plan: Recommend formal diagnostic evaluation, psychoeducation, support linkage; continue safety monitoring.
